claim: The court's final judgment bars Google from exclusive distribution contracts for Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, and the Gemini app, but explicitly does not bar Google from paying distribution partners like Apple for preloading, placement, or default status.
stance_target: exact remedy terms applicable to Apple
scope_conditions: US v. Google, D.D.C. Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM, Document 1436, final judgment, Sept 2 2025
quoted_support: Google will be barred from entering or maintaining any exclusive contract relating to the distribution of Google Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, and the Gemini app... Google will not be barred from making payments or offering other consideration to distribution partners for preloading or placement of Google Search, Chrome, or its GenAI products. Cutting off payments from Google almost certainly will impose substantial -- in some cases, crippling -- downstream harms to distribution partners, related markets, and consumers, which counsels against a broad payment ban.

claim: The court explicitly modified the final judgment to prohibit Google from entering an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product in any Safari mode or on any Apple device.
stance_target: Apple-specific operative remedy language extending to GenAI/Gemini deals
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies opinion, Section III.L modification, internal p.114
quoted_support: And to leave no doubt that Apple falls within the revision, Section III.L of Google's RPFJ shall be modified to make clear that Google is prohibited from entering into an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product either in any Safari mode or on any Apple mobile or desktop device.

claim: Browser Developer agreements (covering Apple/Safari) must allow the developer to annually set a different general search engine at various access points across devices, as a condition of receiving Google's revenue share.
stance_target: annual rebidding is the operative legal mechanism, not merely a commentator's characterization
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies opinion, RPFJ Section III.K-L
quoted_support: Google also would be permitted to pay Browser Developers, including Apple, to set Search as the default GSE, so long as the Browser Developer (1) can promote other GSEs and (2) is permitted to set a different GSE on different operating system versions or in a privacy mode and makes changes, if desired, on an annual basis.

claim: The court's own liability findings establish that in 2021 Google paid more than $26 billion in traffic acquisition costs to distribution partners, and that figure 'has likely grown since' -- this is a court-adjudicated figure, not an analyst estimate, though it covers all distribution partners, not Apple alone.
stance_target: dollar magnitude of Google TAC payments
scope_conditions: US v. Google, 747 F. Supp. 3d at 88-89 P289 (2024 liability findings), cited in 2025 remedies opinion
quoted_support: In 2021, Google paid more than $26 billion in "traffic acquisition costs" to distribution partners. That number has likely grown since.
numbers: more than $26 billion (2021, all distribution partners combined)

claim: The court found that the prospect of losing tens of billions in guaranteed, nearly-costless revenue from Google disincentivizes Apple from launching its own competing search engine; Apple SVP Eddy Cue's remedies-phase testimony agreed this was a significant disincentive, though he maintained Apple was still unlikely to enter search.
stance_target: why Apple has not built a competing search engine despite capability
scope_conditions: liability opinion at 168; remedies-phase testimony of Eddy Cue
quoted_support: The court found that "[t]he prospect of losing tens of billions in guaranteed revenue from Google -- which presently come at little to no cost to Apple -- disincentivizes Apple from launching its own search engine when it otherwise has built the capacity to do so." ... Cue] agree[d]... "that it was a disincentive for [Apple] to do a search engine based on the payments that [Apple was] receiving from Google. . . . It's a significant amount of money."

claim: The court rejected Plaintiffs' expert Dr. Chipty's prediction that a full payment ban could shift 31% of query share to Google's competitors and increase the chance of Apple entering general search, finding the estimate 'too speculative and not grounded in realistic assumptions about market behavior.'
stance_target: quantified structural-erosion thesis for a full payment ban scenario
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies opinion, rejection of Dr. Chipty's share-shifting model
quoted_support: Although not essential to its conclusion, the court did not find Dr. Chipty's share-shifting exercise to be persuasive. The potential 31% market shift of queries to competitors struck the court as too speculative and not grounded in realistic assumptions about market behavior.

claim: The final judgment has a six-year term, effective 60 days after entry (except Technical Committee provisions, effective immediately); Plaintiffs sought up to 10 years, Google sought 3 years.
stance_target: duration of the remedy regime relative to the query's 2-5 year holding horizon
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies opinion, judgment duration
quoted_support: The term of that judgment will be six years, and it will become effective 60 days after entry, except for those provisions relating to the Technical Committee, which will go into effect immediately.

claim: RSAs can no longer offer higher revenue-share percentages conditioned on exclusive-tier device placement; previously nearly all RSA-covered devices were enrolled at the highest-revenue tier, locking in Google as the only preloaded GSE.
stance_target: non-exclusivity provisions structurally change the pricing mechanism of default deals, not just cosmetically
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies opinion, RSA revenue-share tier provision
quoted_support: RSAs can no longer offer higher revenue share percentages for exclusive tiers... "Nearly all RSA-covered devices are presently enrolled at the highest-revenue tier, thus locking in Google as [the] only preloaded GSE."

claim: The court found that AI has unquestionably improved general search but has not yet fundamentally altered market dynamics, citing evidence that Bing gained no new distribution or market share despite closing the AI-driven quality gap, and that AI-native entrant Neeva exited the market for lack of distribution.
stance_target: generative AI competition alone will rapidly erode Google's distribution dominance within the query's 2-5 year horizon
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies opinion, findings on AI's competitive impact
quoted_support: AI has unquestionably improved general search, but it has not yet fundamentally altered market dynamics.

claim: As of December 2024, Apple began integrating ChatGPT/OpenAI technology into Apple Intelligence in exchange for revenue share payments to Apple, and Apple's Safari search query volume declined for the first time in 22 years, an event Apple executive Eddy Cue linked partly to the emergence of generative AI alternatives.
stance_target: evidence that alternative AI providers already pay Apple and that Google's default position faces some erosion pressure
quoted_support: In December 2024, Apple began integrating ChatGPT and OpenAI technology into its devices to power Apple Intelligence, Apple's AI experience integrated into its devices, in exchange for revenue share payments... Apple's own witness, Apple executive Eddy Cue, testified that the volume of Google Search queries in Apple's Safari web browser had declined for the first time in 22 years likely due to the emergence [of GenAI alternatives].
